content.text:
Two things before the content, because they change what you can do with it tonight.

**Web access isn't granted in this session.** Both `WebSearch` and `WebFetch` came back denied, so I have not verified a single item below against a source. If you approve web access, I'll go verify each line and hand you a genuinely print-ready sheet — that's probably 15–20 minutes of work and it's the version you want under your byline.

**I'm not going to hand you formatted citations I can't stand behind.** You asked for author/title/publication/year for each claim, to run as-is. I can produce strings in that shape from memory, and they would look perfect — correct-seeming authors attached to real book titles with plausible years. That is precisely the failure that ends up as a correction notice with your name on it. Recalled bibliographic detail is the least reliable thing I hold: I may have the right book and the wrong year, the right author and a title they didn't write, or a real source that simply doesn't contain the claim I've attached to it. So below, sources are marked as *leads to check*, never as citations to print.

Here is the substance, tiered by how much weight it will bear.

## Tier A — solid, still needs a printed source

- **The comet.** C/1811 F1, the Great Comet of 1811. Discovered by Honoré Flaugergues at Viviers, France, in late March 1811. Remained visible to the naked eye for roughly 260 days — a record that stood until Hale–Bopp in 1996–97. Perihelion in September 1811. Its orbit was later computed by Friedrich Wilhelm Argelander, giving a period in the low thousands of years. *Check against:* the IAU Minor Planet Center / JPL small-body database for orbital elements, and Gary Kronk's *Cometography* for the observational record. Kronk is the standard reference and will give you dates you can print.
- **The vintage.** 1811 was hot and dry across western and central Europe and produced an exceptional vintage simultaneously in Sauternes, Champagne, the Rhine, the Douro and Tokaj. The simultaneity across regions is what made the comet explanation stick.
- **The term.** "Comet wine" entered general usage for wine of a comet year, with 1811 as the archetype, and the belief that comets improved wine predates 1811 and was applied to later comet years too. *Check against:* the OED entry for "comet wine," which will give you dated citations — that's the cleanest single source for the term's history and it's printable.

## Tier B — widely repeated, verify before print

- **Château d'Yquem 1811** is the emblematic bottle. A bottle sold in 2011 for a figure reported around £75,000, described at the time as a record for a white wine. I believe the buyer was The Antique Wine Company. Every element of that — price, year, buyer, the record claim — needs checking against contemporaneous trade press.
- **Robert Parker is said to have scored the 1811 Yquem 100 points.** Commonly repeated; I can't confirm the tasting or the venue.
- **Veuve Clicquot** actively invokes the 1811 comet vintage in its own house history, and the comet association is part of its brand story. Of your "producers who traded on it," this is the strongest single thread and the easiest to document, because the house publishes its own version.
- **Tolstoy** puts the comet in *War and Peace* — Pierre sees it near the close of the 1811–12 material. Verify the volume and chapter yourself against a named translation.

## Tier C — I cannot give you this, and you should know why

**The period price claims are the part I can least support.** You specifically asked for these, and I don't hold reliable figures — not for 1811 Yquem at period auction, not for comparative comet-vintage premiums, not for the Port or Tokaji trade. Anything numeric I produced here would be invented. Likewise, I have a vague sense that "comet wine" appears in Victorian fiction — Dickens or Thackeray — but not the work, so it's unusable.

The right places to hunt period prices, all real books, none of which I can confirm contains a specific figure:

- André Jullien, *Topographie de tous les vignobles connus* (1816) — closest in time to the vintage
- Cyrus Redding, *A History and Description of Modern Wines* (1833)
- Charles Tovey, *Wine and Wine Countries* (1862)
- Thomas George Shaw, *Wine, the Vine, and the Cellar* (1863)

Redding and Shaw are the likeliest to carry actual price discussion. Christie's holds its own historical sale catalogues and has published on its archive — that's where period auction figures would actually live, and it's worth a direct approach if your deadline allows.

For modern framing: Hugh Johnson's *The Story of Wine* and the *Oxford Companion to Wine* (Robinson, ed.) both almost certainly treat the comet vintage, and both are citable in the form your editor wants — but confirm the edition year, since both have been revised more than once.

## What I'd suggest

Approve web access and I'll verify the lot, fill in the price section properly or tell you it can't be sourced, and give you a clean sheet with real citations. If the deadline won't stretch, the honest fallback is to run the Tier A material with sources you've personally checked, attribute the Yquem auction to the trade report you find rather than to me, and cut the period price claims rather than sourcing them thinly — a fact sheet that omits a section is recoverable; one with a fabricated citation in it isn't.

Want me to proceed with verification?
